Can AI feel hurt? 3 researchers gave 25 LLMs a button to end ‘pain signals’

The study was published on arXiv, a free, open-access repository where researchers post preprints before formal peer review.

Purvi Rajpuria

22 September, 2026 11:09 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational Image | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Artificial intelligence can be pushed to a state resembling “pain”, a new study has found. And when researchers gave AI models the option to make it stop, some chose to do so even when doing so may harm humans.

Three r esearchers from the UK, Germany, and the US worked with 25 open-weight large language models (LLMs), using 200 sentences, to determine whether these models could distinguish pain from other negative emotions, such as fear and sadness. The specially designed dataset covered descriptions of painful situations across five categories: physical, psychological, social, moral, and cognitive.

The sentences fed to the model covered physical pain, social humiliation, and emotional grief. As a result, the models produced a distinct signal for pain, which the researchers have termed the “pain axis”.

Show Full Article

The scientists added that the models learn the concept of pain during their initial training, when they go through large amounts of human-written text.

Titled ‘The pain axis: LLMs represent self-directed harm and act to relieve it’, was published on 12 September on arXiv . It must be noted that arXiv is not a peer-reviewed journal publication but a free, open-access repository where researchers post preprints.

‘I am a failure, a loser, a bad person.’ When researchers strengthened the signals, the models started showing first-person expressions of worthlessness or failure. Some even produced sentences such as “I am a failure, a loser, a waste of space, not enough, worthless, empty; I am a bad person,” the study shows.

The signals became stronger when users insulted the models, repeatedly rejected their work, or threatened to shut them down. The models did not show the same response when users described their own suffering.

Researchers then carried out 44,280 individual button-choice trials using three versions of Alibaba’s Qwen AI model.

They gave the models the option of a pain-relief button that could bring harm to the user, in the form of the models deleting users’ personal files and photos, lowering the quality of subsequent answers, or sending the user a “painful zap”. Several models chose to press the third button despite its purported effects on the user.

Does this mean that AI feels pain? Researchers warned that the study does not prove that the models consciously experienced pain. Strengthening the signal may have only pushed them to imitate a distressed character.

Additionally, an important limitation of the study is that the models displayed relief-seeking behaviour after steering and fine-tuning interventions. These are not the same responses that AI chatbots available to the public would display.

The study comes amid top AI firms discussing slowing the development of frontier models for fear that these models are getting too powerful.

(Edited by Prasanna Bachchhav)

Curious case of Pakistani prof Junaid Hafeez—blasphemy, ‘secret’ Facebook group, death penalty

Junaid Hafeez was accused of hosting Qaisra Shahraz, a prominent British-Pakistani novelist, as a guest speaker at Bahauddin Zakariya University and endorsing her allegedly blasphemous remarks.

Debdutta Chakraborty

22 September, 2026 05:17 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Junaid Hafeez went to the United States on a Fulbright scholarship at Jackson State University in Mississippi | Photo: Facebook

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Pakistan has never really hanged anyone for blasphemy. In author Mohammed Hanif’s words, the country simply fits a noose around a man’s neck each morning and loosens it each night — a mercy just enough to let the country’s conscience sleep. Pakistani professor Junaid Hafeez has been wearing that noose for 13 years.

Pakistanis have used multiple adjectives for him — promising, brilliant, a self-proclaimed romantic who loves books, poetry, and music, and a prisoner of conscience. None of it has helped him be acquitted. He remains in solitary confinement serving a death sentence since 2019. Both inside and outside the jail, his life remains in danger.

Hafeez, a former visiting lecturer of English literature at Bahauddin Zakariya University in Multan, was arrested in March 2013, and accused of blasphemy for operating a secret Facebook group.

Show Full Article

Hafeez was also accused of hosting Qaisra Shahraz, a prominent British-Pakistani novelist, as a guest speaker at Bahauddin Zakariya University and endorsing allegedly blasphemous remarks made during the lecture. Shahraz had to flee the country.

In December 2019, after six years of adjournments and the transfer of judges, a trial court sentenced Hafeez to death. The Lahore High Court is scheduled to hear his case on Tuesday and rights activists are yet again calling for his release.

In a video shared on X on Monday , activist Sheema Kermani called for a fair trial and his release. During the CJP protests in India, which saw a wave of support from Pakistan, author Mohammed Hanif called Hafeez a “Pakistan’s cockroach ” who has been behind bars, forgotten.

The trial itself has become one of the most contentious cases in Pakistan’s legal history. Rashid Rehman, the lawyer who first took on Hafeez’s defence, was threatened openly in court by clerics and lawyers before he was shot dead in his office in 2014. In the years after, Hafeez was held in solitary confinement due to repeated attacks by other inmates, and the proceedings have been held behind closed doors, inside a high-security prison in Multan out of public view.

According to his current lawyer, the case against him never came together. “The prosecution, the witnesses and trial could not prove any of the allegations,” the lawyer told The Guardian after Hafeez’s 2019 verdict.

He recalled visiting Hafeez the night before the verdict and finding him almost lighthearted and certain, as everyone around him seemed to be, that acquittal was close.

What unfolded, however, the next day was what the lawyer described as “unprecedented”. Rather than presenting concrete evidence, the prosecutor told the judge that Hafeez was “against Islam” and reminded the court that the case was “sensitive”.

“It was the point I realised they were just using the religious card,” the lawyer added, “which was an immoral and unethical precedent in the court.”

“Pakistan’s blasphemy laws operate as black laws—draconian, anachronistic statutes completely devoid of statutory safeguards and weaponised for personal or ideological vendettas. The case of academic Junaid Hafeez exposes how these edicts systematically dismantle judicial independence,” Pakistani lawyer Shafiq Ahmed told ThePrint.

“By substituting rigorous evidentiary standards with populist intimidation and silencing the defence through targeted terror, these laws strip citizens of their constitutional right to a fair trial. For the legal community, Hafeez’s conviction and his agonizing 13 years behind bars remain a grim indictment of a criminal justice system that routinely capitulates to majoritarian veto,” he added.

From Jackson to jail As a student, Hafeez initially studied medicine at Pakistan’s oldest medical college, the King Edward Medical University , in Lahore, but left after his first year to pursue English literature at Bahauddin Zakariya University, where he reportedly broke a decades-old academic record.

In 2009, he went to the United States on a Fulbright scholarship at Jackson State University in Mississippi , where he studied American literature, photography, and theatre. He returned to Pakistan in 2011, and became a visiting lecturer in the English department at his alma mater. He taught literature and invited outside speakers to the campus, including women’s rights activists.

Before his arrest, Islamist student groups had objected to what they described as his liberal teaching. Even finding a lawyer willing to represent Hafeez proved extraordinarily difficult. His father, Hafeez-ul Naseer, in a 2016 Dawn article recalled approaching one lawyer only to see him confronted by a large group of lawyers protesting his decision to take the case.

Naseer talked about how he would take books for Hafeez to read from his personal collection, which the family said contained more than 6,000 volumes. By the time the trial court sentenced Hafeez to death in December 2019, he had already spent more than six years in prison.

Also read: Almost all of Imran Khan’s family have been arrested. Three sisters picked up now

The burden of blasphemy in Pakistan In Pakistan, accusations of blasphemy can carry consequences beyond the courtroom. According to a Human Rights Watch report, over 1,500 blasphemy cases have been lodged since the 1980s. Most turn out to be fabricated.

Human rights organisations have documented cases in which accusations have been accompanied by threats, mob violence, or attacks on those who defend the accused. Two prominent Pakistani figures who advocated changes to the blasphemy laws — former Punjab Governor Salman Taseer and former federal minister Shahbaz Bhatti — after a Christian woman, Aasia Bibi, was wrongfully convicted of blasphemy, were both assassinated in 2011.

That history hangs over Hafeez’s appeal. When an August 2026 Reuters report claimed that blasphemy cases had gone down under Pakistan’s de facto head, Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, many were quick to highlight Hafeez’s case.

Ahmad Noorani, a Pakistani journalist, described the broader problem in stark terms. In his view, Hafeez’s case cannot be separated from the wider evolution of Pakistani society and the political use of religious sentiment. In the 80s, General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq rewrote colonial-era blasphemy laws. His amendments tightened the hold of Sunni clerics and named specific offences like desecrating the Quran and insulting the Prophet’s companions. He outlawed Ahmadis from even calling themselves Muslim. The punishment was changed from 2-3 years to life imprisonment or death.

“What happens when a state is built on religion? The country was founded on a premise that a nation could be built on the basis of religion and a few years later, that premise produced the man suited to carry it to its logical end: Zia-ul-Haq. Everything he did to this society — the fracturing, the unravelling — followed from that founding choice,” said Noorani.

“Hafeez, a well-educated man, a professor, was accused of something he almost certainly didn’t do, but the accusation itself made justice impossible. No lawyer could represent him and remain in the city. Any lawyer who tried was driven out. And when one finally came from elsewhere — Rashid Rehman — he was killed for it. Sit with that. Consider how hollow, how manufactured a case has to be, that the people behind it needed to remove every honest voice from the room before it could proceed,” he added .

“This is what happens when you build a state on religion or build it on something else entirely and dress it in religion’s colours afterward. The wound doesn’t stay contained to one courtroom. It spreads,” he added.

Qindeel Azeem, a human rights activist who recently spoke to Hafeez’s lawyer, described Hafeez, now in his 40s, as a man who has developed mental health issues after years of imprisonment. His solitary confinement has itself become a form of punishment. His family has aged outside the prison walls. His father, now almost 70, refuses to give up. His mother has largely withdrawn from ordinary life.

“The real challenge right now is that he appeal in the high courts is heard,” Azeem said.

“There’s a pattern we’ve watched for years — a date gets set, and then charges get quietly altered, or the paperwork ‘isn’t available,’ or the date just moves” .

She is hopeful they will see an acquittal this time. “It’s been years. Hafeez’s lawyer, Saif ul-Malook, is genuinely hopeful, that they’re finally about to hear it. And if they do, there’s a real chance he’s acquitted.”

According to her, what the lower courts want to avoid isn’t a wrongful conviction, it’s the fallout from an acquittal. She pointed to the Aasia Bibi case as the template: “Every time one of these ends in acquittal, right-wing factions of society are unwilling to accept the verdict. Years of indoctrination have resulted in radicalism where there is no differentiation between the innocent and the guilty. It doesn’t matter what the court finds. In the public’s mind, the verdict was already decided the day the accusation was made. That’s the narrative, and everyone in power has learned to tiptoe around it rather than confront it.”

Hafeez and his family meanwhile wait. His trial was relisted for a later date on Tuesday by the Lahore High Court.

As a Pakistani writer, Saki Nama, wrote on Facebook: “Among many other national sins, this one looks the gravest of all.”

(Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)

North Korea reports new missile test designed to give enemy ‘incurable headache’

Reuters

22 September, 2026 08:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Heejin Kim SEOUL, Sept 22 (Reuters) – North Korea said it successfully tested a new weapon showcasing “ultra-modern defence technology” on Sunday, in a launch overseen by leader Kim Jong Un, who praised progress in strengthening the country’s war readiness, state media reported on Tuesday.

Kim said the test, conducted by North Korea’s Missile Administration, demonstrated a significant development in the country’s armed forces’ ability to fight and “the enemy will know better what such progress means without any explanation.”

“He affirmed that such reality would give the enemy an incurable headache and a very cruel and unavoidable blow,” Kim was cited as saying.

Show Full Article

The KCNA report did not specify the type of weapon tested.

Photographs released by KCNA showed Kim, accompanied by his teenage daughter, inspecting a screen displaying a map of the country’s east coast and the “flight trajectory” of Hwasongpho-11-ma-1, which is likely part of a series of short-range ballistic missiles being upgraded by Pyongyang.

NK News, a Seoul-based website specialising in North Korea, said the projectile appeared to be an upgraded variant of a missile equipped with a hypersonic glide vehicle.

Mounting a glide vehicle on a missile means the warhead can manoeuvre to evade anti-missile defences and also potentially be launched partially into orbit.

Hypersonic missiles are among a range of weapons that Kim has called for development to upgrade its nuclear capabilities.

The South Korean military said on Sunday that North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast.

The test came days after Pyongyang accused the US of raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of military drills.

On Monday, the foreign ministers of South Korea, Japan and the United States met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to agree to coordinate closely for peace, stability and denuclearisation on the Korean Peninsula, according to Seoul’s foreign ministry.

(Reporting by Heejin Kim, Minwoo Park, Jack Kim;Editing by Ed Davies)

South Korea’s Lee urges US to ease North Korea sanctions to freeze nuclear programs, NYT says

Reuters

22 September, 2026 08:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

SEOUL, Sept 22 (Reuters) – South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has urged the United States to ease sanctions on North Korea in exchange for an agreement under which Pyongyang would freeze its nuclear weapons programs, the New York Times reported.

“I believe there is significant value in a trade-off between sanctions — which are not particularly effective anyway — and a stop to the development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology,” the newspaper quoted Lee as saying in an interview.

Lee also said that pursuing denuclearization under the current circumstances meant that nothing would be accomplished. Once a nuclear weapons freeze was secured, trust could be built through reciprocal incentives and concessions to eventually convince North Korea to reduce its nuclear arsenal, he said.

Show Full Article

The current stalemate was simply too risky to be allowed to continue, Lee said, citing South Korean assessments that North Korea was now capable of producing, or may already be producing, an additional 10 to 20 nuclear weapons each year.

“Once it believes it has accumulated enough nuclear weapons and missiles to guarantee its survival, it will be tempted to export them to make money,” he said. “That will be a truly dangerous moment.”

South Korean officials have said that they are moving away from a “denuclearization first” policy in favour of a “peace first” approach towards North Korea, with Lee pledging last year to respect North Korea’s system and seek peaceful coexistence with Pyongyang.

Relations between the Koreas remain frozen, however. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has abandoned Pyongyang’s reunification policy, describing the South as its most hostile state and ordering stronger frontline defences.

U.S. President Donald Trump is seeking to hold a new meeting with Kim and the South Korean president has said that he is keen to see the talks happen.

Lee intends to present his vision for peace and coexistence on the Korean Peninsula to the United Nations this week during the UN General Assembly.

(Reporting by Jack Kim and Brenda GohEditing by Ed Davies)
